definition: A unit of ownership in a company. Owning shares makes you a part-owner (shareholder) of that company.
example: If a company has 1,000 shares and you own 25, you own 2.5% of it.

definition: A person or organisation that owns shares in a company. Ordinary shareholders can usually vote at the general meeting and may receive dividends.
Ownership in a company. In investing, "equities" is the formal word for stocks. On a balance sheet, equity is what belongs to the owners: assets minus liabilities.
A payment a company makes to its shareholders, usually out of its profits. Dividends are not guaranteed: the company decides whether to pay one and how much.
example: A company pays a dividend of €2 per share. If you own 50 shares, you receive €100 (before taxes).

definition: The profit you make when you sell an investment for more than you paid for it. Selling for less than you paid is a capital loss.
example: You buy a share for €80 and sell it for €100: a capital gain of €20 (before fees and taxes).

definition: The total market value of a company's shares: the share price multiplied by the number of shares.
example: 1,000,000 shares at €50 each = a market capitalisation of €50 million.

definition: The meeting of a company's shareholders, usually held once a year, where shareholders can vote on important matters such as electing board members or approving a dividend.
Spreading your money across many different investments (for example many companies, sectors and countries) so that a problem with one of them does less damage to the whole.
A debt security: a loan from an investor to a company or government. The issuer pays interest during the bond's life and repays the face value when it matures.
example: You buy a 5-year bond for €1,000 paying 4% a year: you receive €40 interest each year and €1,000 back after 5 years, if the issuer can pay.

definition: Money that is borrowed and must be paid back, usually with interest. For a company, loans and bonds are debt; for an investor, buying a bond means lending money (holding debt).
A person or organisation that is owed money, for example a bank that gave a loan or an investor who holds a bond. Creditors are paid before shareholders if a company is liquidated.
The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year. Borrowers pay it; lenders and savers receive it.
example: €1,000 at an interest rate of 3% earns €30 in one year.

definition: Where new securities are issued for the first time and the issuer (a company or government) receives the money, for example in an IPO.
Where investors trade existing securities with each other, for example on a stock exchange. The company that issued the shares does not receive money from these trades.
Initial public offering: the first time a company sells its shares to the public and has them listed on a stock exchange.
The rule that shareholders of companies such as an AG are not personally liable for the company's debts. The most a shareholder can lose is what they paid for their shares.
A type of share that usually has no voting rights but receives dividends before ordinary shares and ranks ahead of them if the company is liquidated.
A tradable investment instrument, such as a stock or a bond.
A short code, usually a few letters, that a stock exchange uses for a listed security. Tickers are not unique across exchanges.
A 12-character code that identifies one security worldwide: a 2-letter country code, a 9-character basic number and a check digit. In Austria, ISINs are assigned by the OeKB.
A six-character German securities identification code. It has largely been replaced by the ISIN but is still widely used in German-speaking countries.
An organised, regulated marketplace where securities of listed companies are traded under fixed rules. Today trading is almost entirely electronic.
Under the EU's MiFID II rules: a regulated market, a multilateral trading facility (MTF) or an organised trading facility (OTF).
Multilateral trading facility: an EU trading venue, run by an investment firm or market operator, that brings many buyers and sellers together under fixed rules, similar to an exchange.
Over-the-counter: trading directly between two parties instead of on a trading venue. In the US, 'OTC securities' are securities not listed on a national securities exchange.
A number that tracks the prices of a selected group of shares, such as Austria's ATX. News reports often call it 'the market'.
A private person who buys and sells investments with their own money, for themselves.
A professional organisation that pools money and invests it on behalf of others, such as pension funds, investment funds, insurance companies and banks.
A firm that stands ready to buy or sell a security at publicly quoted prices, making it easier for others to trade at any time.
A firm that buys and sells securities on behalf of its clients and usually holds them in the client's account. Retail investors reach the market through a broker.
A general rise in prices over time, which means the same amount of money buys less.
example: If prices rise 3% in a year, something that cost €100 now costs €103.

definition: How strongly and how often an investment's price moves up and down. More volatile means bigger swings in both directions.
A group of investments that behave in similar ways, such as stocks, bonds, cash or property.
The money (or other assets) that owners contribute to a corporation in exchange for shares. In an Austrian AG it is called Grundkapital and is divided into shares.
The German and Austrian name for a stock corporation: a company with its own legal personality whose share capital is divided into shares. In Austria the minimum share capital is €70,000.

Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung: a limited liability company common in Austria, Germany and Switzerland. In Austria it needs at least €10,000 of share capital; its ownership stakes are not traded on stock exchanges.
Austria's commercial register. A GmbH or AG only comes into existence when it is entered in the Firmenbuch.
The nominal amount printed on a share (in Austria at least €1 for par value shares). It is an accounting figure and says nothing about the market price.
A share without a nominal amount; each share represents an equal fraction of the share capital.
A share whose owner is recorded by name in the company's share register. In Austria, unlisted AGs must issue registered shares.
A share whose owner is not recorded by name in a company register.
The company's list of the names of holders of registered shares. In Austria (Aktienbuch), only the person entered counts as a shareholder towards the company.
The maximum number of shares a company is allowed to issue under its founding documents. Issued shares are those actually handed out.
Capitalisation table: a list of everyone who holds a company's shares and related securities (such as options and convertible notes), with how many and on which terms.
The reduction in existing owners' percentage when a company issues new shares. Owners keep the same number of shares, but each is a smaller slice.
example: You own 100 of 1,000 shares (10%). The company issues 250 new shares: you now own 100 of 1,250 (8%).

definition: What a company is considered to be worth, as estimated by analysts or agreed between a company and its investors.
A company's value before new money from a funding round is added.
A company's value right after a funding round: pre-money valuation plus the new money. The investor's share equals the investment divided by the post-money valuation.
example: €4 million pre-money + €1 million investment = €5 million post-money; the investor owns €1m ÷ €5m = 20%.

definition: A wealthy individual who invests their own money directly in young companies, typically in early funding rounds.
Money from venture capital (VC) funds: private funds that invest in fast-growing young companies in exchange for equity, usually preferred shares.
Typically a company's first formal funding round, often from friends and family, angel investors or early-stage funds, frequently using convertible notes or SAFEs.
A later funding round, named in order (Series A, Series B, Series C...), often led by venture capital funds.
A loan to a young company that converts into shares (usually preferred shares) at a later funding round or other agreed event. Common in seed rounds.
Often shortened to SAFE: an agreement in which a company promises an investor shares in the future if certain events happen, such as a later funding round.
An investor's right to be paid before other shareholders when the company is sold or wound up, often expressed as a multiple of the investment (1x, 2x).
The right, but not the obligation, to buy a certain number of the company's shares at a fixed price (the strike price), usually after a vesting period.
The process by which an employee gradually earns the right to stock options or shares, for example by staying with the company for a set time.
Raising money from many private individuals, each investing small amounts, usually through an online platform. Investments are often unsecured and carry a high risk of loss.
The official offering document for a public offer of securities, describing the company, its business, finances, risks and the terms of the offer. In Austria it must be approved by the FMA.
An investment bank that manages and sells a securities offering such as an IPO for the issuing company. The lead bank is often called the bookrunner.
Collecting investors' orders (how many shares, up to what price) during an offer's subscription period, to help set the final offer price.
A series of presentations in which a company's management presents an offer to potential investors.
An option allowing the underwriting banks to buy additional shares at the offer price to cover over-allotted shares. Under EU rules it may not exceed 15% of the original offer.
Purchases by the underwriting banks after an offer to support the share price. In the EU, for a share IPO it must end within 30 calendar days and never above the offer price.
An agreement that stops company insiders and large shareholders from selling their shares for a period after an IPO. Most US lock-ups last 180 days, though terms vary.
In the US, the period around the registration of an offering when the company must make sure its public communications about the offer comply with securities laws.
When investors order more shares in an offer than are available, so orders have to be scaled down.
Newly issued shares sold in an offering; the money goes to the company.
Existing shares sold in an offering by current owners; the money goes to those sellers, not to the company.
Admitting a company's existing shares to trading on an exchange without a traditional underwritten IPO; the opening price is found by the market.
Special purpose acquisition company: a shell company with no business of its own that goes public, raises money and then merges with a private company (the de-SPAC transaction).
A way of going public in which a private company merges into an existing listed shell company and takes it over, without a traditional IPO.
When a company separates a division into a new, independent company and gives the new company's shares to its own shareholders.
The part of a company's shares that is available for trading by the public, excluding long-term holdings of founders, families, governments or strategic owners.
When an IPO's offer price is set below the price at which the shares start trading, giving IPO buyers an immediate gain.
Selling shares received in an IPO immediately after trading starts.
An institution that records securities in an electronic book-entry system and keeps them safe. In Austria: OeKB CSD.
Holding securities as electronic account entries instead of paper certificates. Ownership changes by changing the entries.
A bank or firm that holds securities in safekeeping for its clients.
When a company issues new shares to raise money. Existing shareholders are diluted unless they buy their share of the new shares.
A capital increase in which existing shareholders get the first right to buy the new shares, in proportion to what they already own.
A procedure that lets a majority shareholder force the remaining minority shareholders out against a cash payment. In Austria the threshold is 90%.
When a company's shares are removed from a stock exchange. The shares still exist, but become much harder to trade.
When one company or investor acquires control of another company, usually by buying most or all of its shares.
